message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, the evidence doesn't support saying the hours cut is necessary. The question is open, and the report itself says so.

- **No study tested it.** The trial had no arm that cut meetings while keeping full hours, so nothing compares that option against a reduced-hours arm.
- **The only relevant evidence points the other way, weakly.** The two control offices that cut meetings without changing hours gained 4.1% per hour. That is two offices with no comparison group, so it proves nothing. But it suggests part of the gain may be available without reducing hours, which is the opposite of the claim.
- **About half the gain ran through meetings.** The registered mediation analysis attributed 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain to fewer meetings. That makes "reorganisation alone" a serious alternative, not a ruled-out one.

What the evidence can't tell us is whether the hours cut is what makes meeting cuts happen and stick. That would be a reason to keep the hours cut even if reorganisation does most of the work. It's a reasonable hypothesis, but it isn't established.

Suggested wording:

> "The evidence does not establish whether the hours reduction itself is necessary. About half the per-hour gain came through fewer recurring meetings, and two offices that cut meetings without reducing hours saw a smaller gain (4.1%), though this was unplanned and uncontrolled. Whether reorganising work alone would capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes that reorganisation happen, is untested."

If the board needs an answer, the way to get one is a comparison: some teams cut hours, some cut meetings only at full hours, and some carry on as before.
